biz.verdict: The document is honest about how thin the demand is, and its counts and quotes hold up. On business viability it is not yet decision-ready for /replica-launch, for four reasons. (1) There is no cost model in dollars. The storage figure leaves out the second (streaming) copy that F6 keeps, and the egress figure leaves out streaming of FLAC originals on paid plans. (2) The free quota is never sized, even though storage is now the only paid lever. (3) The four proof points were checked against self-hosting and the original, not against the three zero-setup lockers that cap the price (iBroadcast, VOX, YouTube Music). (4) The waitlist gate names no metric, no traffic rule, no decision owner and no plan for a failed test. Angle A is defensible only as a hypothesis to test. Two counter-cases are under-weighted: a hosted backend that serves existing Subsonic apps is the cheaper way to test the "no server" bet, and the case for not building at all (tiny locker audiences on the App Store, Amazon shutting its locker, Google giving uploads away free) should be stated, with "stop" as a real outcome. My dollar figures below are estimates from public list prices that I did not verify this session; the App Store rating counts come from the iTunes Lookup API, fetched 2026-10-04. No files were edited.

issues.section: §7 For /replica-launch (Costs bullet); also F7 policy and the JSON 'Export library on demand' note
issues.sentence: Costs (market lens bitrate arithmetic, not measured): 10,000 tracks ≈ 96 GB as 320 kbps MP3 or ≈ 300 GB as FLAC; 2 hours a day at 320 kbps ≈ 8.6 GB/month of egress.
issues.problem: The §7 figures are labelled as arithmetic, which is good. The same 96–300 GB figure appears without a label in F7 ('storing 96–300 GB per 10,000 tracks') and in the JSON export note. The arithmetic is also incomplete for the product the document specifies. F6 keeps the original bit for bit and also stores a separate transcoded streaming copy, so a FLAC library takes about 380–400 GB per 10,000 tracks, not 300. Paid plans add 'original-quality streaming' and F6 says 'Stream the stored original when the plan and network allow it'. At roughly 1,000 kbps that is about 27 GB/month of egress, not 8.6. A whole-library download is 77–300 GB per device, and none of these is turned into dollars. Without a price per GB, /replica-launch cannot test VOX's $4.99 unlimited plan, set storage tiers, or price the landing-page test. The cost model is handed to /replica-architect, but the landing-page test runs first and should show a price.
issues.replacement: Costs (estimates, not measured: bitrate arithmetic plus public list prices to re-check before pricing): a 10,000-track library is about 96 GB as 320 kbps MP3, or about 300 GB as FLAC plus 77–96 GB for the streaming copy F6 keeps (about 380–400 GB in all). At roughly $6–7 (Backblaze B2-class) to $23 (AWS S3 Standard) per TB-month, storage costs about $0.60–2.20 a month for the MP3 library and $2.30–9.20 for the FLAC one. Egress costs $0 (providers with free egress) to about $0.09/GB (AWS). Two hours a day is about 8.6 GB/month at 320 kbps ($0–0.80), but about 27 GB/month for FLAC originals on an original-quality plan ($0–2.40). A whole-library download is 77–300 GB per device ($0–27 each, one-off). App Store and Google Play keep 15–30% of in-app subscriptions ($0.75–1.50 of $4.99). So at VOX's $4.99, a 10,000-track FLAC collector loses money on S3-class storage and leaves a thin margin on B2-class storage. A 50,000-track FLAC library (the Plexamp reviewer's size) costs about $11–46 a month to store. /replica-architect picks the storage and egress provider, and prices it per GB, before the landing page shows any price. Price by storage tier, never 'unlimited'. In F7 and the JSON export note, add '(estimate; plus the streaming copy)' after '96–300 GB per 10,000 tracks'.

issues.section: §7 For /replica-launch (free tier bullet); F5; F7 policy
issues.sentence: The free tier is limited by storage, not by playback controls (F1, an internal policy). Paid plans add storage, original-quality streaming, seats and more download devices (F5).
issues.problem: Every playback control is free (F1) and downloads are on every plan (F5). That reverses recon's 'mobile with offline as the paid hook', so storage is the only paid lever that scales with cost, and the free quota becomes the single most important pricing decision. The document never sizes it and never flags it as a decision. The free rivals set expectations high: YouTube Music allows 100k uploads free (about 960 GB at 320 kbps by the document's own arithmetic) and iBroadcast states no fees. F7 also lets a cancelled user keep a library within the quota indefinitely ('Only account deletion ... or a shutdown after notice deletes the whole library'). There is no inactivity rule, so free-tier storage grows with every dormant account, with no revenue against it.
issues.replacement: Add after the sentence: "Storage is the only lever that scales with cost, so the free quota is the main pricing decision. /replica-launch sets it as a number (GB or tracks) from the cost model and records: the monthly cost of one free user at that quota, an assumed free-to-paid ratio, and the resulting free-tier cost carried by each paying user. tunebox will not out-give the free rivals on storage (YouTube Music: 100k uploads free, about 960 GB at 320 kbps; iBroadcast: no fees), so the free tier is a trial size, not a competitor to them. Add an inactivity rule to F7 (for example notice by email, then deletion after a stated period with no sign-in, with export open throughout). Amend F7's 'Only account deletion ... deletes the whole library' to include it, and cover it in the bounded keep-claim."

issues.section: §6 Angle A, proof points (and proof point 1)
issues.sentence: Each proof point is matched by someone on its own. The bet is the combination without a server, and that bet is what the waitlist test checks.
issues.problem: Proof point 1 ('Zero setup, no server') is measured only against Plexamp, Navidrome and Amperfy. iBroadcast (free), VOX ($4.99) and YouTube Music uploads (free) also need no server, and they are the products the document says cap the price. So 'without a server' separates tunebox from self-hosting only. For the 'combination' to be a difference, it has to be checked against those three, and it was not. The market file does not record whether any of them exports audio and playlists, shows personal play counts, has live smart playlists or shuffles once per cycle (F4 already says 'unverified against lockers'). VOX's official App Store listing (2026-09-28, fetched again via iTunes Lookup) lists CarPlay, Sonos, Last.fm scrobbling and queue management. For cloud sync it names only Mac, iPhone, iPad and Windows, with no Android or web client mentioned. That points to a possible real difference against the paid anchor (Android and web), and to a gap (the car 'skip'). The document mentions neither.
issues.replacement: "Without a server separates tunebox only from self-hosting: iBroadcast (free), VOX ($4.99) and YouTube Music uploads (free) need no server either. The bet is the combination against those three, and it is unverified. Before the landing page is written, check the current iBroadcast, VOX and YouTube Music apps for: export of audio files and playlists, personal play counts, live smart playlists, once-per-cycle shuffle, and supported platforms. Take any proof point that one of them already ships off the landing page. VOX's official listing (2026-09-28) names Mac, iPhone, iPad and Windows for its cloud sync and mentions no Android or web client, so Android plus web is a candidate difference against the paid anchor. It lists CarPlay and Sonos, so the car-integration skip (section 5) is a gap against it."

issues.section: §6 HARD GATE (also §5 'Hard gate' and §7 first bullet)
issues.sentence: a threshold that /replica-launch sets and records before the test runs. If it fails, stop or re-position; the evidence here cannot size the market.
issues.problem: The gate is not decision-ready. (a) No metric: a free email signup cannot tell tunebox apart from free iBroadcast or YouTube Music uploads, so it does not test whether anyone will pay. (b) No price is required on the page. (c) No traffic rule: traffic from Hacker News would reproduce the HN-heavy, ownership-searched sample bias that the document itself warns about. (d) No minimum sample or duration. (e) No human decision owner: a skill drafts the threshold, but the founder has to own the decision. (f) Nothing collected for the cost model: library size and format at signup would replace the market lens's guesses. (g) 'Re-position' has no named target. (h) §5 says both 'the test runs first' and 'the thin vertical slice ... is built first'. F1–F4 and F8 (including M-sized F4 with its cross-device PlaybackState) are 'not gated', so work can be sunk before a result that might say 'stop'.
issues.replacement: "HARD GATE: no L-sized storage, transcode or offline work (F5, the F6 bulk and transcode pipeline, F7's full-file export) starts until a landing-page test passes. /replica-launch drafts the gate spec and the founder approves and records it before launch. (1) The page shows the price and storage tiers set from the cost model (section 7) and only the proof points that survive the locker check. (2) The primary metric is the share of unique visitors who make a paid commitment (a refundable deposit, or 'reserve at $X/month' with a card). Email signups are secondary. (3) Traffic comes from at least two channels other than Hacker News, with a minimum number of unique visitors per channel and a minimum run (for example 4 weeks), both set in advance. (4) The form asks library size (tracks or GB), main format (MP3/AAC/FLAC) and what the person uses now, and the answers feed the cost model. (5) Pass, ambiguous and fail are written down in advance as numbers. Pass: build the slice, then F1–F4 and F8, then the gated items. Ambiguous: one re-run with changed price or copy. Fail: stop, or re-test the cheaper Subsonic-compatible backend (section 5) before any native build. Nothing beyond the landing page is built until the result is recorded." In §5, change "The thin vertical slice ... is built first" to "The thin vertical slice ... is built first after the gate result is recorded".

issues.section: §5 Flagged, not in the top 8 (Subsonic-compatible API); same reasoning in the §1 disagreement table and the §6 Recommendation
issues.sentence: Its evidence is HN-only and thin, the same as A's upload demand, so by a consistent thin rule it is not dismissed.
issues.problem: This is a category error. The Subsonic-compatible API is a way of delivering the product, not a claim about demand, so the thin rule does not apply to it. It should be judged on build cost and time to first revenue, and on those terms it is the strongest counter-case to the plan. A hosted backend with web upload and a Subsonic-compatible API lets existing clients (Substreamer free, Symfonium paid, Amperfy) supply iOS and Android playback and their own offline downloads. That takes F5 (L) and recon's 'playback engine on 3 platforms' and 'offline downloads on mobile' hard parts off the path to the first paying users. It also fits what owners already name (Plex 12, Navidrome 8, Jellyfin 6, Subsonic family 4) and the 21 HN commenters who already run such stacks. Treating it as a side option means /replica-architect will size a native build before the cheaper test has been considered.
issues.replacement: "Subsonic-compatible API (about M): a delivery option, not a demand claim, so the thin rule does not apply to it. /replica-architect decides on it before sizing native mobile. A hosted backend with web upload and a Subsonic-compatible API lets existing clients (Substreamer free, Symfonium paid, Amperfy; official listings) supply iOS and Android playback and their own offline downloads. That takes F5 and the three-platform playback engine off the path to the first paying users, and it matches what owners already use (Plex 12, Navidrome 8, Jellyfin 6, Subsonic family 4 mentions). Costs: less control of brand and UX; client setup (server URL and login in a third-party app); small client audiences (US App Store ratings on 2026-10-04: Substreamer 141, Amperfy 143); and F4 and F8 differences shown only in tunebox's own web app. It is the fallback if the waitlist result is ambiguous or fails." In §1 and §6, replace "is HN-only and thin, exactly like A's upload demand, so it is kept" with "is a delivery option evaluated on cost and time to test, and is kept".

issues.section: §4 U1 (market facts) and §6 Risks; F7 Evidence
issues.sentence: Hosted lockers exist but are small: iBroadcast is free with no ads; VOX is $4.99/month with unlimited storage.
issues.problem: 'Small' is stated with no data behind it, and the document never states the case against building at all. Cheap proxies for market size were available this session, because the iTunes Lookup endpoint worked. On 2026-10-04 the US App Store showed 325 ratings for iBroadcast, 3,154 for VOX (the whole player, not only its cloud) and 10,146 for Plexamp. Amazon closed its music storage service (2017), and Google keeps uploads only as a free feature (Google Play Music, now YouTube Music). The document reads those two exits only as 'why a locker has to earn trust' (F7), not as a sign that consumers rarely pay separately for a locker. Together with HN-only demand and a target segment of heavy-storage collectors, this is a substantive case for not building. A reader deciding whether to spend a quarter on an L-sized build should see it, and the gate threshold should be set to beat it.
issues.replacement: U1: "Hosted lockers exist and look small: on 2026-10-04 the US App Store showed 325 ratings for iBroadcast and 3,154 for VOX (its whole player, not only its cloud), against 10,146 for Plexamp (iTunes Lookup API; ratings, not users). iBroadcast is free with no ads; VOX Premium is $4.99/month with unlimited cloud storage." Add to §6 Risks: "The strongest case against building: the large companies that tried did not keep a paid locker (Amazon closed its storage service in 2017; Google offers uploads only as a free feature), the lockers that survive are small or free, demand outside HN is unmeasured, and tunebox's target is the heaviest storage users. The waitlist threshold is set to beat this case, and 'stop' is an acceptable outcome."

legal.verdict: The research side holds up, but the legal and billing hand-off needs fixes first: 8 material issues. Quotes, counts and the original's name rules hold up. §7 Legal is clearly labelled "not legal advice; review with counsel", F5 and F7 send their open questions to counsel, and no review is used as a testimonial. The problems are elsewhere. (1) In-app purchase rules are tied only to a paid offline option, when they cover every paid plan. (2) The no-audio-streaming sharing decision and the F5/F7 policies never reach /replica-architect. It reads only recon.md and features.csv, and recon.md still says "public links stream only". fixes.md also says features.csv is untouched, but commit efebd5a applied all 9 rows, including one with an unbounded notice promise. (3) "Removed after a copyright notice" rules out restoring the file after a counter-notice. (4) F7's "Only … deletes the whole library" and its N-day notice box in terminations and give repeat infringers notice. (5) Nothing stops cross-user deduplication, which would undercut the per-user-copy position a private locker relies on. (6) The sharing bullet misdescribes MP3tunes and states "0 share-keyword hits", which is false (13 rows use the word). (7) The legal frame is US-only, while the sample covers GB, IE, CA, NZ and AU. (8) /replica-launch's default "problem" section would pull the ads and free-tier themes, which reads as a catalogue promise. Legal points below are background for counsel and were not verified this session.

issues.section: §7 For /replica-launch (also F5 'Skill' line and §7 Costs bullet)
issues.sentence: Paid plans add storage, original-quality streaming, seats and more download devices (F5). Decide whether any part of offline is paid; if so, resolve the conflict with YouTube Music's free offline uploads and apply the App Store and Google Play in-app purchase rules.
issues.problem: This reads as if store billing rules only matter if offline is paid. In fact every paid plan (storage, quality, seats, device cap) is a digital subscription once it is sold or unlocked inside the iOS/Android app (Apple guideline 3.1.1/3.1.3, Google Play Payments policy). The plan design as written breaks those rules or ignores them in four ways. (a) The recon upsells (F07 'free user (upsell to S23)', F09 'quota meter / offline toggle upsell -> S23 -> checkout', S18 'quota exceeded') lead to a hosted Stripe checkout from inside the app, and /replica-backend's default is Stripe only. (b) The recommended test, 'storage-based pricing (pay for the space used)', can't be sold through Apple or Google subscriptions, which are fixed-price products per period. (c) 'One-page cancel … on the cancel screen' and the F7 cancel rule can't apply to subscribers billed by the store: they cancel and get refunds in the store's settings, and tunebox only learns of it through server notifications. (d) The recon Subscription model has a single provider_customer_id.
issues.replacement: Paid plans add storage, original-quality streaming, seats and more download devices (F5). Every paid plan, not only paid offline, is a digital subscription once it is sold or unlocked in the iOS or Android app. Choose one route before /replica-architect and /replica-backend run: (1) sell the same plans in the apps through Apple in-app purchase and Google Play Billing, as fixed tiers (store subscriptions cannot bill per GB used, so 'pay for the space used' is web-only or becomes tiers), next to Stripe on the web, with one entitlement record fed by all three providers; or (2) ship the mobile apps as companions with no price, purchase button or upgrade call to action, except in storefronts and programs that currently allow external purchase links. The upsells in recon F07, F09 and S18 follow that choice. Store-billed subscribers cancel in the store, so the one-page cancel applies to web billing, and the F7 cancel rule runs from the stores' server notifications. Check the current Apple App Review Guidelines 3.1 and the Google Play Payments policy, including the US and EU variants, at build time. Separately, decide whether any part of offline is paid; if so, resolve the conflict with YouTube Music's free offline uploads.

issues.section: §7 Legal (sharing bullet) and F7 policy; §1 'Where the audit trail lives'; §5 intro; §8 A3; analysis/features-rows.final.json 'Export library on demand' (now features.csv line 69)
issues.sentence: "This changes recon F08 and S25, where a recipient 'plays (if public)'." / "This changes the recon F09 edge 'read-only until under' …" / "features.csv is read-only in this phase; proposed rows and notes are in `analysis/features-rows.final.json`." / "features.csv is still not edited in this phase." / JSON and features.csv: "Copy: always exportable with N days notice before any deletion or shutdown, plus the DMCA caveat"
issues.problem: The main legal mitigation (no streaming of a user's audio to anyone else) and the F5/F7 policies live only in fixes.md. /replica-architect reads only recon.md and features.csv (.claude/skills/replica-architect/SKILL.md line 15). recon.md is unchanged on these points: its Legal note still prescribes 'public links stream only', F08 'plays (if public)', F07 '(mobile, paid)' with an upsell, F09 'read-only until under', and Size says 'offline as the paid hook'. The architect gets contradictory inputs. fixes.md also says features.csv is untouched, but commit efebd5a applied all 9 rows and notes (features.csv now has 82 rows, and recon.md says '/replica-entrepreneur added 9 rows'). The applied Export row still carries the unbounded 'N days notice before any deletion or shutdown' copy that audit C1 removed everywhere else. C1 only fixed the Plan and billing note.
issues.replacement: §7 Legal: "This overrides recon F08, S25 and recon's Legal note ('public links stream only'). /replica-architect reads only recon.md and features.csv, so update those lines, F07 ('paid', upsell), F09 ('read-only until under') and the Size line ('offline as the paid hook') in recon.md before it runs." §1 and §5: "The rows and notes in `analysis/features-rows.final.json` were applied to features.csv in commit efebd5a (82 rows)." Delete "features.csv is still not edited in this phase" from A3. Export row note, in the JSON and features.csv: "Copy: always exportable, with N days' notice and working export before any deletion for plan reasons, a user's own account deletion, or a shutdown; files taken down after a copyright notice follow the notice-and-takedown process (section 7); never say never held hostage."

issues.section: §7 Legal (DMCA bullet); same wording in §2 item 14, U2, F5, §7 keep-claim bullet, JSON 'Keep stored copy bit for bit' and 'Download for offline on mobile'
issues.sentence: "DMCA and uploads: keep `Report content (copyright),social,must`, F11 and S26. Also needed: a designated DMCA agent, a counter-notice process and a repeat-infringer policy." together with "it is removed after a valid copyright notice" / F5: "when the file leaves the library: … or it is removed after a valid copyright notice"
issues.problem: The document requires a counter-notice process, but it describes a takedown as the file being removed and 'leaving the library', and backend and architect will build that as deletion. Under 17 U.S.C. §512(g)(2)(C) the provider has to put the material back 10–14 business days after a valid counter-notice unless the claimant reports a court action. A deleted file cannot be put back, so the counter-notice process cannot be honoured. The recon model already has Track.status 'taken_down', which fits disabling access rather than deleting. Two US safe-harbour basics are also missing. A designated agent only counts once it is registered in the US Copyright Office's online directory, and the registration lapses after three years unless renewed. §512(i) also requires that users are told about the repeat-infringer policy.
issues.replacement: "Notice and takedown (not legal advice; counsel to confirm). Register the designated agent in the US Copyright Office DMCA directory, list it on the site, and renew it every three years. Publish the repeat-infringer policy in the terms. A takedown disables access (Track.status = taken_down; device copies are removed at next connection) and keeps the stored copy, so it can be restored after a valid counter-notice under §512(g). Counsel sets when a taken-down copy may be deleted." Everywhere else, replace "it is removed after a valid copyright notice" with "access to it is disabled after a valid copyright notice".

issues.section: F7 policy (same text in §6 Angle A, proof point 3, F7 Wording, JSON/features.csv 'Plan and billing management'); F7 heading
issues.sentence: "Only account deletion (by the user, or termination under the repeat-infringer policy) or a shutdown after notice deletes the whole library; a user-requested deletion offers an export first. Before any deletion tunebox makes for plan or account reasons, or a shutdown, tunebox gives N days' notice and keeps export working throughout" and the heading "Your library is always exportable, with notice before any deletion"
issues.problem: The wording works as a promise that boxes tunebox in. (a) 'Only' rules out terminating for any other breach of the terms (fraud, chargebacks, abuse, malware, illegal non-copyright content, court orders). (b) A termination under the repeat-infringer policy is an 'account reason', so the text promises a repeat infringer N days' notice with export working, and it says nothing about whether uploads, playback, downloads and sharing go on during those days. §512(i) requires that termination actually be carried out. (c) Content that must be removed or kept for the authorities cannot be offered for export. (d) The heading promises notice before any deletion, including deletions the user makes and takedowns.
issues.replacement: Heading: "F7. Your library is exportable on demand, with notice before plan-driven deletion (rescoped)." Policy: "The whole library is deleted only when the user deletes the account, when the account is terminated under the terms (including the repeat-infringer policy), or when the service shuts down after notice; a user-requested deletion offers an export first. Before a deletion for plan reasons, a user's own account deletion or a shutdown, tunebox gives N days' notice and keeps export working throughout. A termination under the terms or the repeat-infringer policy stops uploads, playback, sharing and downloads at once. Counsel decides whether, and for how long, the user may export files that are not subject to a notice; nothing is exported where the law requires removal or preservation. Files taken down after a copyright notice follow the notice-and-takedown process (section 7)." In §6 and the Plan and billing note, replace "for plan or account reasons" with "for plan reasons, a user's own account deletion".

issues.section: F6 Build or change; §7 For /replica-architect (storage cost model)
issues.sentence: "Detect duplicates by checksum (`Track.checksum` is already in the model)." / "Own the storage cost model for originals plus streaming copies (F6)"
issues.problem: The document stresses storage cost ('96–300 GB per 10,000 tracks', '"Unlimited" storage is a real risk'). Content-addressed deduplication across users is the obvious saving, and nothing rules it out. Storing one master copy and streaming it to every account that uploaded the same file weakens the private-locker position, which rests on each user streaming their own copy (the unique-copy reasoning in Cartoon Network v. CSC Holdings, 2d Cir. 2008; the unlicensed lockers of 2011 stored a copy per user for this reason; background, not verified this session). It also tangles takedowns: disabling one stored object would hit every account that shares it. The tracklist-only sharing rule ('matched by checksum') has the same exposure if a match ends up serving the sharer's stored object.
issues.replacement: F6: "Detect duplicates by checksum within one user's library only. Store and stream each user's own uploaded copy, with no deduplication across users, and never serve one account's stored file to another, even when checksums match (not legal advice: the private-locker position rests on per-user copies; counsel confirms before the cost model assumes any deduplication)." §7 For /replica-architect: "Own the storage cost model for originals plus streaming copies (F6), assuming no deduplication across users."

issues.sentence: "Why: public streaming of uploaded audio is the largest copyright exposure, and the data show no demand for it (0 requests to share uploads in the owner set, and 0 share-keyword hits across all 1227 rows; fit check). Background, not verified in this session: … music lockers that streamed uploads to others (MP3tunes, Grooveshark) were sued."
issues.problem: Three problems. (1) '0 share-keyword hits across all 1227 rows' is false. reviews.csv has 13 rows containing share/shared/sharing, and some praise sharing music, e.g. app-store 5★ 2026-10-02 'share music through messages', app-store 5★ 2026-08-24 'share the jams', HN 2023-07-29 'share Spotify links with friends and play Music League'. The fit check (verify-fit.md line 41) says something narrower: a net for sharing one's uploads found 0. (2) MP3tunes was mostly a private locker, not one that streamed uploads to others. On appeal its repeat-infringer policy was faulted for ignoring users who copied infringing files for their own use (EMI v. MP3tunes, 2d Cir. 2016). Using it as an example of public streaming suggests that private-only means low risk, which is the wrong lesson for tunebox's own repeat-infringer policy. (3) 'Tracklist only' leaves open whether the public S25 view (recon: 'Header', playlist cover 'auto mosaic or custom upload') shows the owner's uploaded cover art or custom images. That would be public display of the owner's uploads.
issues.replacement: "Why: public streaming of uploaded audio is the largest copyright exposure, and the data show no demand for it (0 requests to share uploaded files in the owner set, and a sharing-uploads net over all 1227 rows found 0; fit check. 13 rows use the word 'share'; the few about sharing music praise sending catalogue links or Jam sessions, which tracklist-only sharing won't reproduce, so most rows a recipient opens will be greyed out). The shared view shows text only (titles, artists, albums, durations), never the owner's cover art, custom playlist cover or lyrics. Background, not verified in this session: Grooveshark, which streamed user uploads to the public, was sued and shut down; MP3tunes, a mostly private locker, was also sued, and on appeal its repeat-infringer policy was faulted for ignoring users who copied infringing files for their own use, so even a private locker needs an enforced repeat-infringer policy."

issues.section: §7 Legal; the 'DMCA process' carve-outs in F7, §6 Angle A and proof point 3
issues.sentence: "files removed after a valid copyright notice follow the DMCA process instead (section 7)" / "(copyright takedowns follow the DMCA process)" / "DMCA and uploads: keep `Report content (copyright),social,must`, F11 and S26."
issues.problem: The whole legal frame and every bounded promise point to 'the DMCA process', which is US law. The research sample is 5 of 6 storefronts outside the US (nz, ca, gb, ie, au), and the document never names launch countries. For EU users, a hosting service has duties under the Digital Services Act no matter its size: notice-and-action for any illegal content, not just copyright (Art. 16), a statement of reasons to the uploader when content is removed (Art. 17), points of contact (Art. 11–12) and, for a company outside the EU, an EU legal representative (Art. 13). Canada uses notice-and-notice. S26 is a copyright-only form, and uploads include user images (embedded cover art, custom playlist covers), so non-copyright reports are needed as well. Background, not verified this session.
issues.replacement: §7 Legal, new first bullet: "Launch countries decide the takedown regime (not legal advice). /replica-launch names the launch countries and counsel maps each one: US DMCA §512 (registered agent, counter-notice, published repeat-infringer policy); EU Digital Services Act Art. 11–17 (notice-and-action for any illegal content, a statement of reasons to the uploader, points of contact, an EU legal representative if tunebox has no EU establishment); Canada's notice-and-notice; others as counsel advises. S26 accepts non-copyright reports too (uploads include cover images)." Everywhere else, replace "follow the DMCA process" with "follow the notice-and-takedown process (section 7)".

issues.sentence: "Listing and pricing copy must not name the original or quote any reviewer." (the only landing-copy rule in the /replica-launch notes)
issues.problem: /replica-launch builds the landing page's 'The problem' section from 'the top two "hate" themes' (.claude/skills/replica-launch/SKILL.md, Step 1.2).
